title: The 24-Hour Rule of Celebration and Mourning
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership presents Pat Summitt's 24-hour rule as a tool for keeping ego in check. Summitt limited celebration after wins and mourning after losses to one day, believing that beyond that, vanity, pride and ego were extending the emotion and distracting the team. The post argues that this discipline builds the humility and concentration needed to prepare for the next contest. It does not deny people the right to feel; leaders should give space to learn and process. The bounded window reminds people to move on rather than live in the past, and the author recommends it for individuals and teams.
points: Pride distorts performance in both directions: excessive self-criticism after setbacks and self-satisfaction after wins.
Summitt limited elation and lamentation to 24 hours, then required players to refocus.
The author attributes emotion lasting beyond a day to vanity, pride and ego.
Time-limiting emotion trains humility and concentration for the next challenge.
Leaders should still grant space to process results; the rule bounds the time rather than banning feeling.
quotes: Those who strive for excellence often become too self-critical after defeat or a setback, and too self-satisfied after a victory or achievement.

Known as the 24-hour rule, Summitt insisted that players limit their elation and lamentation to one day. After that, she claimed, it was vanity, pride, and ego that extended the flood of emotions and would derail the team if left unabated.
If Coach Summitt saw any player focused on victory or defeat more than 24 hours later, she would insist they jettison the emotions and get back to work.

By limiting the time players or team members have to explore their emotions and thoughts after a critical contest or outcome, they learn to embrace the humility and concentration required to prepare for the next competition without much thought to the last one.

Team members want and deserve the time to work through the thoughts and emotions that come with success and setback. This is only natural and good leaders give them the space and time to learn from what just happened and to explore how this makes them feel.
But limiting that time in a reasonable way reminds team members to move on and not live or play in the past.
